summary:
We developed AstroTrade, an interactive, educational space mission design game that
simulates the entire systems engineering lifecycle—from concept to operation. The
solution directly addresses the NASA Space Apps challenge by bridging the gap
between academic theory and practical decision-making. In the game, participants
navigate real-world aerospace trade-offs, balancing mass, power consumption,
budget, data rates, and orbit while selecting scientific instruments and launch vehicles.

project uses the four fundamental mission segments to structure its simulation logic. It
is significant because it democratizes the study of systems engineering, allowing

details:
What the project does: AstroTrade is an interactive, educational space mission design game that simulates the complete systems engineering lifecycle of a satellite or CubeSat—from initial concept to operation. It allows players to define scientific objectives, choose orbits, select payload instruments, and determine the appropriate launch vehicle. How it works: The system operates using a rules engine based on real-world engineering trade-offs. As the user modifies spacecraft components—such as adding a heavier or more complex instrument—the game calculates, in real time, the impact on critica
resources: mass, power, budget, data rate, and orbit. If limits are exceeded (for example, if the spacecraft is too heavy for the chosen rocket), the simulation flags the error and requires the player to adjust the design. The underlying logic is inspired by NASA’s four fundamental mission segments and the *CubeSat 101* guidelines. Benefits: - Transforms abstract theoretical concepts in space engineering into a practical, visual, and interactive experience. - Teaches systems thinking and the management of limited resources. - Provides immediate feedback, helping students understand the "why" behind a project’s success or failure. What we aim to achieve: To democratize access to aerospace engineering education, sparking interest among students and enthusiasts in solving complex problems through a playful and collaborative approach. Technologies and Tools Used: - Frontend / Interface: HTML - Logic and Simulation: HTML * - References and Data: *CubeSat 101* guidelines, NASA’s Concept Maturity Levels (CMLs), and the Mission Design Lab (MDL) architecture.
